failures.title: Aston Martin M177HYB Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Oil Cooler Hose Failure - Oil Leak / Smoke Risk - 20,000-60,000 miles
items.whatHappens: Aston Martin issued a recall for 1,095 vehicles in the US market due to a potential oil cooler hose failure on the Mercedes-AMG M177 engine. The engine oil cooler hose may split and leak oil, leading to oil loss, low oil pressure warnings, and potential smoke in the engine compartment. This condition affects DBX707, DB12 and Vantage models equipped with the M177 engine.
items.repairVsReplace: Oil cooler hose replacement is a specialist job. Affected owners will be notified and repairs carried out free of charge under recall. If the hose has already failed, oil contamination may require additional cleaning and component inspection. Budget £800-£1,500 for diagnosis and repair.

items.title: Ignition Coil Degradation - Misfire / Rough Running - 30,000-70,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The M177's ignition coil packs are mounted in the hot-V area, where heat from the twin turbos can cause premature degradation. Water ingress into the spark plug shafts has also been reported, causing coils to short out. Symptoms include misfires under load, rough idling, and check engine light illumination.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil pack replacement is a labour-intensive job on the M177 family. Specialists recommend replacing all eight coil packs and spark plugs as preventative maintenance at 50,000-60,000 miles. Budget £2,000-£3,500 for the full job.

items.title: Carbon Build-Up on Intake Valves - Misfire / Performance Loss - 40,000-80,000 miles
items.whatHappens: Modern direct-injection engines like the M177 do not spray fuel over the intake valves, so oil blow-by and carbon deposits accumulate over time, causing future misfires or valve sealing issues. This is a well-documented issue on the M177 engine family.
items.repairVsReplace: Walnut blasting or media blasting to clean the intake valves is the standard solution. Budget £500-£1,000 for the cleaning procedure.

failures.goodYearsLine: The M177HYB benefits from the extensive development and refinement of the M177 family. Aston Martin has addressed the oil cooler hose issue with a recall, and later production units benefit from improved components. Regular maintenance and preventative coil pack replacement are key to longevity.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the M177HYB
variants.intro: The M177HYB is a plug-in hybrid evolution of Aston Martin's 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8. It combines the M177 4.0L V8 engine with an electric motor for a total system output that exceeds 800 bhp. The engine itself is believed to produce around 727 bhp (727 PS), with the electric motor contributing additional power. Where to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on the block - typically on a machined pad near the front of the engine. The code is listed as M177 on technical documentation. It also appears on your V5C logbook. Commonly confused codes: - M177 - the standard Mercedes-AMG 4.0L twin-turbo V8 used in C63, E63 and G63; wet-sump lubrication, no hybrid system - M178 - the Aston Martin variant of the M177 used in Vantage and DB11 V8; bespoke tuning, different ancillaries, no hybrid system - M176 - the mainstream Mercedes 4.0L V8 used in non-AMG models; lower output and different tuning Why fitting the wrong revision matters: The M177HYB is a highly specialised variant with a unique plug-in hybrid system. The ECU calibration, electric motor integration, cooling system, and ancillaries all differ significantly from standard M177 applications. Fitting the wrong spec will result in incorrect fuelling, boost control, hybrid system incompatibility, and potentially engine damage.

relatives.description: M177 (DBX 707): - the standard 4.0L twin-turbo V8 used in the DBX 707, producing 697 bhp. The M177HYB is a significant evolution - it adds a plug-in hybrid system for 800+ bhp total output, making it the most powerful Aston Martin production vehicle powertrain ever.

M177 (Mercedes - AMG): - the M177HYB shares its core V8 architecture with the M177 used in Mercedes-AMG C63, E63, G63 and GT63 models. However, the M177HYB features a unique PHEV system with Aston Martin-specific calibration and integration.
M176: - the mainstream Mercedes 4.0L V8 used in non-AMG models (S560, GLS580). It produces 469 bhp and shares the same block architecture but has different cylinder heads, turbos and calibration.

AMG GT 63 S E Performance: The same M177-based PHEV architecture is used in the Mercedes-AMG GT 63 S E Performance, combining the M177 V8 with an electric motor for over 800 bhp. However, Aston Martin applies bespoke tuning and a different hybrid system integration. An engine page is pending for these applications.

relatives.code: Bentley PHEV V8: Bentley uses a related 4.0L V8 PHEV system in the Flying Spur and Bentayga Hybrid, based on the same M176/M177 family. However, these are lower
relatives.description: output versions and not directly comparable to the M177HYB.

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used M177HYB makes sense only with full documented service history and confirmation that the oil cooler hose recall has been addressed. Given the high value of the cars these engines sit in and the complexity of the PHEV system, specialist inspection is absolutely essential before purchase. Used engines guide

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper M177HYB recon addresses the oil cooler hoses, ignition coil packs, intake valve carbon cleaning, and all common wear items - plus a full check of the hybrid system components. Reconditioned units from vetted UK specialists come with a 12-24 month warranty and are the default choice for most DBX S PHEV owners. At £22,000-£30,000 supply-only, they offer the best balance of cost and peace of mind. Reconditioned engines guide

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified for high-value collectable examples (low-mileage DBX S PHEV) or where the original engine has matching-numbers value. A proper M177HYB rebuild should include a full bottom-end rebuild, new turbochargers, comprehensive hybrid system check, upgraded cooling system, and all ancillaries. Budget £30,000-£40,000+ for a specialist rebuild. Rebuilt engines guide

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All three options can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK Aston Martin PHEV specialists, with warranties backed by the fitting workshop. Nationwide delivery and fit available. Supply & fit guide
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The M177HYB sits exclusively in vehicles worth £150,000-£250,000+. A reconditioned engine at £22,000-£30,000 represents 10-20% of the vehicle's value, making replacement financially viable across the entire range. The high value of DBX S PHEV models means even the most expensive rebuilt option is justified. That said, given the significant investment and the complexity of the PHEV system, full due diligence - including specialist inspection and thorough service history review - is essential before any purchase decision.

items.answer: Reconditioned M177HYB units start from an estimated £22,000 supply-only, with fitted prices from £23,380-£31,380+ depending on the workshop. Used engines: £15,000-£22,000 supply-only. Rebuilt units: £30,000-£40,000+ supply-only. Labour: 20-28 hours at £65-£91/hr.

items.question: What is the most common problem with the Aston Martin M177HYB engine?
items.answer: Oil cooler hose failure is a known issue - Aston Martin issued a recall for M177-powered vehicles due to potential oil cooler hose splitting, which can cause oil leaks and smoke in the engine compartment. Coil pack degradation and carbon build-up on intake valves are also reported. Oil cooler hose replacement: recall item (free) or £800-£1,500 if out of warranty. Coil pack replacement (all 8): £2,000-£3,500. Intake valve carbon cleaning: £500-£1,000.

items.question: Which Aston Martin models use the M177HYB engine?
items.answer: The M177HYB powers the DBX S PHEV (2025-present) and is expected to be used in future Aston Martin PHEV models. It is Aston Martin's most powerful production powertrain, combining the 4.0L V8 with an electric motor for 800+ bhp total output. [See full compatibility list above]

items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt M177HYB engine?
items.answer: For most owners, a reconditioned M177HYB with oil cooler hose inspection, new coil packs, and full PHEV system check is the best balance of cost and reliability. Used: only with full service history and specialist inspection - recall must be addressed. Reconditioned: default for DBX S PHEV owners, 12-24 month warranty. Rebuilt: for high-value collectable examples (low-mileage DBX S PHEV).

items.question: How do I know if my Aston Martin has the M177HYB engine?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad near the front of the block. The M177HYB is the 4.0L PHEV V8 that powers the DBX S PHEV. Check your V5C logbook, inspect the engine bay near the front of the block, or enter your registration above for instant confirmation. [Check your engine code now]

items.question: What's the difference between the M177HYB and the standard M177?
items.answer: The M177HYB is the plug-in hybrid evolution of the M177. It adds an electric motor and battery system for total output exceeding 800 bhp. The core V8 architecture is the same, but the M177HYB has bespoke ECU calibration, different ancillaries, and a unique PHEV system that makes it significantly more complex to service and replace.
